Wheezing in babies: bronchiolitis and when to get help

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A whistling sound from a baby’s chest can be frightening, particularly during a first cold. A blocked nose can also sound noisy, so the sound alone cannot tell you where the problem is. If you think your baby is wheezing, arrange prompt medical assessment. Look at their breathing effort, feeding, colour and alertness rather than waiting to hear a particular noise.

Breathing signs that need emergency help

Call your local emergency number if your baby is struggling to breathe, has pauses in breathing, looks blue or grey around the lips or tongue, or is floppy or difficult to wake. Skin pulling in beneath the ribs or at the neck, grunting with breaths, head bobbing and very fast breathing can signal serious effort. Do not wait for a fever, for a pause to last a set number of seconds, or for all these signs to appear together.

A baby who is too breathless to feed needs immediate help, not repeated attempts to finish a bottle. Stay with them and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. A breathing problem that suddenly follows food, medicine or an insect sting may be a severe allergic reaction, especially with swelling or floppiness. Do not wait for a rash; use the baby’s prescribed adrenaline auto-injector according to their emergency plan, if available, while calling for help.

Wheeze is different from a blocked-nose sound

Wheeze usually describes a musical or whistling sound as air moves through narrowed smaller airways, often more noticeable while breathing out. Snuffling from the nose and a harsh noise when breathing in may come from higher in the airway. Parents understandably use similar words for these different sounds. A clinician may need to listen to the chest and examine the baby to distinguish them.

Small nasal passages can sound congested, but a newborn’s suspected chest wheeze should not simply be labelled normal. Nor should grunting be dismissed as an ordinary sleep sound when the baby is working to breathe. For a baby who is otherwise stable, note when the noise occurs and whether it changes during feeds or sleep; this helps the assessment. Do not delay getting help to make a recording or to test home remedies.

Why bronchiolitis can make a baby wheeze

Bronchiolitis is a viral illness affecting the tiny breathing tubes in the lungs. Swelling and mucus make it harder for air to pass through. It often begins with a runny nose and mild cough, then develops into faster or harder breathing, chest noises and difficulty feeding. Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common cause, although several other viruses can produce the same illness.

It is especially important in the first year of life, though some services use the term for children under two. A baby may worsen over the first few days after an apparently mild start. Many improve over about a week or two, while the cough can linger for several weeks. These are broad patterns, not a deadline to wait out: increasing effort, reduced feeds or unusual sleepiness needs reassessment whenever it occurs.

Young age and feeding changes matter

Very young babies, babies born prematurely, and those with significant heart, lung, neurological or immune conditions need a lower threshold for assessment. RSV can cause reduced activity, irritability or poor feeding in a young infant without a fever. Tell the clinician about your baby’s birth history and health conditions, even if the breathing noise initially seems mild.

Get immediate medical assessment for a temperature of 38°C or more in a baby under three months, or 39°C or more at three to six months. A very low temperature or a baby who looks seriously unwell also needs immediate help. Seek urgent assessment for worsening symptoms, substantially reduced milk intake or fewer wet nappies; no urine for 12 hours needs immediate assessment. Do not wait for that interval if your baby is already feeding poorly or seems dehydrated.

What else may explain the symptoms?

One episode of wheeze does not establish asthma. Repeated episodes, eczema, family history and symptoms between infections can become relevant as a child grows, but infancy is not a time to assume an asthma diagnosis from the sound alone. Bronchiolitis and later asthma are associated in some studies; this does not mean a particular baby will develop asthma or that the infection is the sole cause.

Pneumonia, whooping cough and other conditions can also cause breathing difficulties. Babies with whooping cough may have pauses in breathing without the familiar whoop or even much cough. Persistent respiratory symptoms together with poor growth or recurrent infections may prompt investigation for less common conditions such as cystic fibrosis. These clues guide an examination; they are not a checklist for diagnosing a disease at home. A new formula or food does not prove allergy merely because noisy breathing follows it.

What happens at the medical assessment?

The clinician will ask when the illness began, how breathing and feeds have changed, and how many wet nappies the baby is having. They will examine breathing effort, listen to the chest and assess hydration and alertness. Oxygen levels may be measured with a suitable clinical sensor. Describe coughing fits, possible choking, contact with someone with a prolonged cough, and any sudden symptoms after a food or medicine.

Typical bronchiolitis is usually diagnosed clinically. A chest X-ray, blood tests or a virus test is not automatically needed for every baby. Tests may be appropriate when the diagnosis is uncertain, the illness is unusually severe or the baby deteriorates unexpectedly. The decision about home or hospital care takes account of feeding, breathing, age and underlying health, as well as whether the family can return promptly if things change.

Keep milk feeds manageable

Once a clinician has agreed that home care is suitable, offer the usual breast milk or infant formula in smaller amounts more frequently. A baby with a blocked nose may tire during a long feed. Watch their comfort and wet nappies rather than trying to force a normal-sized feed through breathlessness. Ask for a specific feeding and review plan if you are unsure how to judge intake, particularly when breastfeeding.

Prepare formula at its usual instructed concentration: extra water or extra powder is not a treatment for illness. Do not replace a young baby’s milk feeds with water, juice or herbal drinks to “loosen mucus”. Older babies may already have age-appropriate water with solids, but milk remains important. If the baby cannot maintain hydration safely by mouth, medical care may include a feeding tube or intravenous fluids; this is not something to manage by diluting bottles.

Nasal saline and suction have limited roles

Clearing a blocked nose may make a feed easier, but it does not remove inflammation deep in the lungs. Ask your clinician whether intermittent plain nasal saline around feeds is appropriate. Gentle, superficial suction may be considered when nasal secretions interfere with feeding or breathing; routine repeated suction and deep suction are not recommended for bronchiolitis.

Have a health professional show you a suitable method and follow the product instructions. Do not push a suction device deep into the nose or keep trying when it causes distress or irritation. Nasal saline is different from medicine delivered to the lungs through an inhaler or nebulizer. Never put albuterol into the nose, mix an inhaled treatment at home, or borrow another child’s medicine because the symptoms sound similar.

Why an inhaler or antibiotic is not the usual answer

Treatment for ordinary bronchiolitis mainly supports breathing and hydration while the illness settles. Albuterol, also called salbutamol, is not routinely used for infant bronchiolitis, even when asthma runs in the family. Steroids, nebulized saline treatments and antibiotics are not routine home remedies either. Antibiotics may be needed for a separate bacterial infection, and a different diagnosis may need a different treatment.

Some babies need hospital oxygen, feeding support or more intensive breathing assistance. Specialists may use additional treatments for particular severe cases; newer guidance includes selected intensive-care situations that do not apply to home treatment. If your baby already has a prescribed medicine plan for another condition, ask the treating team how to use it during this illness. Do not stop, add or change medicines by adapting a bronchiolitis article into a prescription.

Avoid cough mixtures, honey and risky steam treatments

Do not give an infant nonprescription cough or cold medicines, adult preparations or homeopathic cough products. Some can cause serious adverse effects and combination products can accidentally duplicate ingredients. Fever or pain medicine, when appropriate for the baby’s age and circumstances, may improve comfort but does not open narrowed airways. Ask a clinician or pharmacist about the exact product and dose; fever medicine must not delay assessment of a young infant’s fever.

Never give honey to a baby younger than 12 months, including in milk or a soothing drink, because of infant botulism risk. Honey is not a treatment for wheeze. A cool-mist humidifier may ease nasal dryness, but should not be relied on to treat bronchiolitis. If used, follow cleaning and water instructions and avoid damp surroundings; dirty tanks can disperse irritants and microorganisms. Avoid hot steam and bowls of hot water around babies because of burns.

Comfort, sleep and reassessment at home

You can hold your baby more upright while they are awake and you are alert. For sleep, place them on their back on a firm, flat, level surface with a clear sleep space. Do not prop up the mattress, add pillows or use an inclined sleeper to make breathing seem easier. If lying down appears to cause breathing distress, seek medical advice rather than changing to an unsafe sleep position.

Check your baby regularly, including overnight, and use the return precautions given by their clinician. Before leaving an appointment, confirm whom to contact, what changes require immediate help and when a review is due. Being sent home means the baby was considered suitable for home care at that assessment; it does not mean the illness cannot change. A worsening baby needs another assessment even if the diagnosis was already called bronchiolitis.

Reduce exposure and plan follow-up

Keep the home and car free of tobacco smoke and vaping. Wash hands, clean frequently handled surfaces and reduce contact with people who are unwell, especially around a newborn or a baby at higher risk. These steps reduce exposure but cannot prevent every infection. Ask your maternity or child-health team about locally available RSV protection, which may involve vaccination during pregnancy or an antibody injection for the baby; eligibility and timing vary by country.

Arrange follow-up if the cough is not settling as expected, wheeze keeps returning, feeds remain difficult or growth is a concern. Tell the clinician whether the baby becomes completely well between illnesses. Recurrent symptoms may lead to a different assessment, but they do not justify starting an asthma regimen or changing formula without advice. Keeping a brief record of symptoms, feeds and wet nappies can make that discussion more useful.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Infant wheeze assessment considers breathing, hydration, age and underlying health together; a noise or fever measurement alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

Supportive bronchiolitis care differs from an asthma regimen. Selective nasal measures help feeding comfort, while hospital respiratory treatments require clinical supervision.

Families need age-appropriate feeding advice, safe sleep and clear instructions for obtaining another assessment if the illness changes.

How BeMama can help

BEMAMA explains infant breathing and feeding decisions in plain language. Individual examination and local clinical advice determine the diagnosis, treatment and safe place of care.

When to seek help

Call emergency services for breathing distress, pauses, blue or grey colour, floppiness or difficulty waking. Seek immediate assessment for fever of at least 38°C under three months or 39°C at three to six months, or no urine for 12 hours. Seek help earlier for poor feeds or deterioration; do not wait for a threshold if the baby seems seriously unwell.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Suspected wheeze in a baby deserves medical assessment; the sound alone cannot identify the cause.
  • Breathing distress, pauses, blue or grey colour, or difficulty waking require emergency help.
  • Bronchiolitis care usually centres on breathing and feeding support, with clear instructions for reassessment.
  • Offer manageable usual milk feeds; do not dilute formula or use cough mixtures, honey or borrowed inhalers.
  • Nasal comfort measures have limited roles, and safe sleep remains flat and on the back.

Frequently asked questions

When should I get help for a wheezing baby?

Arrange prompt medical assessment for suspected wheeze. Call emergency services for breathing distress, pauses, blue or grey colour, floppiness or difficulty waking. Poor feeding, reduced urine or worsening symptoms also need urgent assessment. A temperature of 38°C or more under three months needs immediate medical assessment.

Can I give honey in milk to stop the wheeze?

No. Never give honey before 12 months because of infant botulism risk, and it does not treat narrowed lower airways. Continue the baby’s usual appropriate milk feeds and seek advice about the breathing problem.

Will a cough or cold medicine help?

Do not give nonprescription cough or cold medicines to an infant. They do not treat bronchiolitis and can cause harm. Age-appropriate fever or pain medicine may sometimes help comfort after advice, but will not relieve airway narrowing.

What causes a baby to wheeze?

Wheeze can occur when air passes through narrowed lower airways. In babies, viral bronchiolitis is an important cause. Nasal congestion and upper-airway sounds can be mistaken for wheeze, and other illnesses are possible, so examination matters.

Does bronchiolitis mean my baby has asthma?

No. One illness does not diagnose asthma, and not every baby with bronchiolitis later develops it. Repeated episodes or symptoms between infections should be reviewed rather than treated using someone else’s asthma plan.

Should I suction the nose every few hours?

Not routinely. When nasal mucus interferes with feeds, ask about a limited trial of saline or gentle superficial suction. Deep or repeated suction can be distressing; these measures do not treat the lung inflammation.

Can my baby sleep propped up during this illness?

No. Place your baby on their back on a firm, flat, level sleep surface without pillows or wedges. Upright holding for comfort is for awake, supervised time. Breathing difficulty needs assessment, not an improvised sleeping position.

Why did the doctor not prescribe antibiotics?

Bronchiolitis is caused by viruses, so routine antibiotics do not help. The clinician may prescribe them if there is a separate bacterial infection. Seek reassessment if the baby worsens; an earlier diagnosis is not a reason to ignore new warning signs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
